stops.name: Porziuncola, the resignation at the Michaelmas chapter
stops.campa: Home from the East, where he heard that his vicars were altering the life, and where the sickness of his eyes began, Francesco gathers the chapter at Saint Mary of the Angels and does the thing no founder does: he lays down the government of his own Order before them all, kneeling, and names Peter Catani, and after Peter's death Brother Elias, to rule in his place. From now on he will command only by example. Henceforth he calls himself simply the little poor man, and asks of the Order one obedience: a brother assigned to be his own superior.
stops.quote: From now on I am dead to you. But here is Brother Peter di Catanio: let us all obey him, you and I.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 11; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 143

stops.name: Gubbio, the wolf at the Vittorina
stops.campa: A wolf of terrible size holds Gubbio in siege; it has eaten beasts and men, and the citizens go armed as to war. Francesco walks out of the gate against all pleading to where the wolf lives, by the place called the Vittorina. The wolf charges, jaws open; Francesco signs the cross and calls him Brother. The wolf closes his mouth, lies at his feet, and by the pledge of a lifted paw contracts the peace: he will harm no one, and Gubbio will feed him door to door. He keeps the pact two years, dies of old age, and is mourned; his grave lies under San Francesco della Pace.
stops.quote: Come here, Brother Wolf. I command you in the name of Christ that you do no harm to me nor to any man. Brother Wolf, since you are willing to make this peace and keep it, I promise you that the men of this town will feed you every day as long as you live, so that you shall never again suffer hunger.

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats
stops.campa: Pentecost, and the plain around the Porziuncola becomes a city of wattle and rush: five thousand brothers encamped in huts of mats, whence the chapter takes its name. Francesco, his voice already failing, has Elias speak for him, sitting at his feet and tugging his tunic when he would add a word. The long Rule of 1221, woven through with the naked Gospel, is read to the multitude. In the crowd sits an unknown young Portuguese, lately of the Augustinian canons: Anthony, whom Padua will claim. The countryside feeds the whole swarm unbidden, and the brothers depart again into all the world.

stops.name: Bologna, the sermon of the Angels, Men and Demons
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption Francesco preaches in the piazza before the Palazzo Comunale of Bologna, city of lawyers, to almost the entire town. A student from Dalmatia, Thomas, later archdeacon of Split, stands in the crowd and writes down what he sees: a man in a ragged habit, unimpressive, unlettered, taking as his theme 'Angels, Men, Demons', and dividing it so finely that the learned marvel, while nobles who have been killing each other for generations make peace on the spot. It is the one sermon of Francesco's life caught by a bystander's pen.

stops.name: Fonte Colombo, the writing of the Rule
stops.campa: In the holy valley of Rieti, on the wooded slope of Fonte Colombo, the Sinai of the Order, Francesco fasts on bread and water with Brother Leo the scribe and Brother Bonizo the jurist, and dictates the final Rule in a cleft of the rock. The ministers climb the mountain to protest its severity; and from the air above the cave Christ's own voice answers them: 'Nothing in this Rule is Francis's; all of it is Mine, and I will that it be kept to the letter, to the letter, without gloss.' The ministers go back down the mountain in silence.

stops.name: Rome, Solet annuere: the Rule confirmed
stops.campa: On 29 November 1223 Pope Honorius III seals the bull Solet annuere and the Rule of the Lesser Brothers passes into the eternal law of the Church: twelve short chapters distilled from fourteen years of Gospel living, argued clause by clause at Cardinal Ugolino's side. What Innocent granted by word of mouth to twelve beggars, Honorius now grants under lead seal to an Order spread from England to Syria. The parchment itself returns to Assisi and lies in the Sacro Convento to this day.
stops.quote: The Rule and life of the Lesser Brothers is this: to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without anything of one's own, and in chastity.
stops.quote_source: Regula bullata, chapter I (the Rule Francis dictated)

stops.name: Greccio, the first nativity
stops.campa: Francesco sends for Giovanni Velita, lord of Greccio: prepare a manger in the cliff-cave, with hay, ox and ass. On the vigil night the mountainside blazes with torches as the people of the valley climb singing to the grotto; Mass is sung over the manger, and Francesco, in the deacon's dalmatic, chants the Gospel and preaches on the Babe of Bethlehem, pronouncing the word 'Bethlehem' like a bleating lamb. Among the pilgrims stands his cousin Pierre Bourlémont, holding the hand of twelve-year-old Joffrey. Giovanni sees a child asleep in the hay wake in Francesco's arms. The hay heals sick beasts; every crib in the world descends from this cave.
stops.quote: I want to enact the memory of that Child who was born in Bethlehem: to see, as far as is possible with my own bodily eyes, the hardship of his infant needs, how he lay in a manger, and how, with an ox and an ass standing by, he rested on hay.

stops.name: La Verna, the seraph and the stigmata
stops.campa: For the fast of Saint Michael, Francesco keeps to Orlando's mountain with Leo and three brothers, lodged alone past a chasm. At the Exaltation of the Cross, praying at dawn, he sees a seraph with six wings of fire descend, and between the wings the figure of the Crucified. When the vision withdraws, the wounds remain: nails of his own flesh through hands and feet, and in his side an open wound that bleeds. The count is his mother's: the Khamsa Pierre sang into Pica, the five sufferings become five wounds. He hides them under bandages; to Leo, who dresses them, he gives the chartula written in his own hand.
stops.quote: You are holy, Lord, the only God, and Your deeds are wonderful. You are strong. You are great. You are the Most High. You are love. You are wisdom. You are humility. You are endurance. You are beauty. You are our eternal life, great and wonderful Lord, God almighty, merciful Savior. — May the Lord bless you and keep you; may He show His face to you and be merciful to you. May the Lord bless you, Brother Leo.
stops.quote_source: The Chartula of Assisi: the Praises of God and the Blessing for Brother Leo, autograph of Francis, written on La Verna, September 1224

stops.name: Borgo San Sepolcro, carried through the town unseeing
stops.campa: Coming down from La Verna on a borrowed donkey, too wounded now to walk far, Francesco passes through Borgo San Sepolcro, where the whole town pours out and the crowd presses to touch him, cutting pieces from his tunic. He notices none of it: rapt out of his senses, he rides through the shouting streets as through an empty field, and only long after, when the brothers speak of the town, does he ask his companions the question the canon treasures as proof of where he truly traveled that day.
stops.quote: When shall we come to Borgo?

stops.name: San Damiano, the Canticle of the Creatures
stops.campa: Nearly blind, his eyes unable to bear daylight or firelight, tormented by field-mice in the night, Francesco lies fifty days in a dark cell of mats beside San Damiano, where Clare and her ladies tend him. There, at the bottom of pain, he is assured in prayer of the kingdom, and rises to compose not a lament but the great doxology of the world: the Canticle of Brother Sun, the first great poem of the Italian tongue, and sets the brothers to sing it. He, who cannot bear the sun on his eyes, praises the sun first of all creatures.
stops.quote: Most High, all-powerful, good Lord, Yours are the praises, the glory, the honor and all blessing. Praised be You, my Lord, with all Your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day, and through whom You give us light; and he is beautiful and radiant with great splendor. Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Moon and the stars. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Wind, and through the air, cloudy and serene, and every weather. Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Water, who is very useful and humble and precious and chaste. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Fire, by whom You light the night. Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Mother Earth, who sustains and governs us, and produces varied fruits with colored flowers and herbs.
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures (Canticle of Brother Sun), composed at San Damiano, 1225

stops.name: La Foresta, the miracle of the vintage
stops.campa: Summoned to Rieti for the treatment of his eyes, Francesco waits at the priest's small church of San Fabiano above the town, and the crowds that come to see the stigmatized saint trample the little vineyard flat and strip the grapes: the priest's whole living. Francesco asks him what the vineyard yields in its best year: thirteen measures. He promises twenty for the ruined vintage. The half-wrecked vines that autumn press out twenty measures of wine and more, and the place takes the name La Foresta and keeps the story with the wine-vat still shown there.

stops.name: Fonte Colombo, Brother Fire and the cautery
stops.campa: The physicians of the papal court at Rieti decree the last remedy for his eyes: the cautery, a rod of iron drawn glowing from temple to eyebrow. At Fonte Colombo the brothers flee the room rather than watch. Francesco addresses the fire in the brazier as an old friend and kinsman, signs it with the cross, and when the searing iron has hissed across his living flesh he calls the brothers back, laughing at them: 'If it is not well burned, let him burn it again.' He has felt, he says, neither the fire's heat nor any pain in his flesh. Brother Fire kept courtesy.
stops.quote: My Brother Fire, noble and useful among all the creatures the Most High has created, be courteous to me in this hour, for I have always loved you and always will for the love of Him who created you. And I pray our Creator who made you, to temper your heat now, so that I may bear it.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 86; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 166
